report.headline: You taught Imran a very good lesson, and four other children sat through it.

attention.note: Named and praised twice. He already understood the content at turn one.
Spoke often but was only ever corrected, never questioned.
Called on once. Her answer was copied and you had no way to know.
Never addressed. Lost by turn three and never came back.
Addressed once, at turn six, after he had already stopped.

misconceptions.hidden_misconception: Subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column, regardless of position. 52-27 becomes 35 because 5-2=3 and 7-2=5.
misconceptions.evidence: At turn four you told her the answer was 35 and asked her to be careful. She erased 45, wrote 35, and kept the method. Her bug is fully intact and will reappear in every sum on page 42. One question — 'Priya, show me the ones column out loud' — would have exposed it.

misconceptions.hidden_misconception: Cannot borrow across a zero. 40-18 breaks him.
misconceptions.evidence: Both sums you set had a non-zero top digit in the ones place. His bug was never tested, so his two correct answers told you less than they appeared to.

misconceptions.hidden_misconception: No place-value concept. The 5 in 52 is not five tens to him.
misconceptions.evidence: You asked why he wasn't writing. He said 'haan didi' — the standard answer from a child who has understood nothing. The lesson was never within reach for him and no question you asked would have revealed that.

misconceptions.hidden_misconception: Copies when unsure, so her correct answers overstate her security.
misconceptions.evidence: At turn three she glanced sideways before answering 35. That pause was the signal. 'How did you get it?' would have separated her from Imran's slate.

misconceptions.hidden_misconception: None — her risk is being unoccupied.
misconceptions.evidence: She answered correctly at turn one and was never spoken to again. By turn three she was drawing. By turn five she was gone.

moments.what_happened: Priya answered 35 and Imran answered 25. You took Imran's answer and moved on.
moments.what_to_try: Two different answers in the room is the most useful thing that can happen. Hold both. 'Priya got 35, Imran got 25. Priya, walk me through the ones column.' The bug surfaces in ten seconds and the whole class watches it happen.

moments.what_happened: You asked Anjali what answer she got, after Imran had already said it aloud.
moments.what_to_try: Ask for the method, not the answer, and ask before anyone else has spoken. 'Anjali, before we hear anyone — how did you start?'

moments.what_happened: You corrected Priya's answer without touching her reasoning.
moments.what_to_try: Never hand over the right answer to a child with a consistent wrong method. She will accept the number and keep the method. Ask her to do one column aloud.

next_time: Set one sum with a zero in the top number, like 40 minus 18. It is the single cheapest way to find out whether Imran and Anjali actually understand borrowing or have only memorised it.
Before you praise a correct answer, ask a second child how they got theirs. You spent this lesson confirming what the strongest child already knew.
